shipped items (Lichess puzzles CC0, and king-and-queen mates); critical and routine are defined here and backed by the mate claims on those items; the half-the-time split is a rule of thumb with no study behind it [H]; the time log is the learner's own evidence

steps.text: In **Where the depth goes: sort the candidates before you calculate** you sorted the moves inside one position. Now sort the **positions**. Given a set and a budget, say 12 minutes for six positions, decide before you start where the minutes go. A forcing line that keeps going gets the most; a position where the first move ends the game gets seconds. Equal shares are the usual mistake.

**When a budget split holds.** It needs a decision that matters and a clock. Rule of thumb: critical positions (checks, a long forcing line, a tempting capture) get about half the time; routine ones get what is left. It fails when you cannot tell which is which in advance, and a sort made after you have solved proves nothing. Stopping is justified by a forced result or a quiet position, not by tiredness.

steps.title: Where the minutes go
steps.prompt: The first position shows a move that works. Then solve the next two. For each of the three, write down in your own words how much of a 12-minute set it would deserve, and what made you say so.

steps.text: **Check your sort.** The first (a mate in 3 by sacrifice) is **critical**: a long forced line, so it earns a lot. The second (a mate in 2, with a tempting rook capture that loses) deserves a **short look**. The third (a queen mate in one) is **routine**: seconds. These three differ in several ways, not one, and its prompt gives the mate away on purpose. In a real set the prompt will not.

steps.text: **The log is the evidence.** The app does not time you; a phone timer does. Take six positions, write plan minutes for each (the six sum to your budget), solve, then write actual minutes. Success means the long plans took the long times and the totals stayed near the budget. Six positions are a rough look, not a measurement. Overspending on a position you marked routine suggests the sort may have been wrong, or that you hesitated; look at which.
